summary: This unit teaches you to manage the risks that a business can create for the environment, and the risks the environment creates for the business. You will learn to identify environmental aspects and impacts, rate risks, keep to permits and the law, choose controls using the hierarchy of control and the waste hierarchy, plan for spills, floods and hurricanes, set targets and indicators, audit, deal with complaints, train staff and learn from incidents.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. Every business has an effect on the environment, through its waste, water, energy, fuel, chemicals, noise, dust and emissions. A manager who does not control these can cause pollution, harm neighbours, break permit conditions, and face clean-up costs, legal action and loss of reputation.

Jamaica's environment is also part of its economy. Beaches, reefs, mangroves, rivers and rainfall support tourism, fishing, farming and water supply. A hurricane, a flood or a drought can damage a business, and a spill from a business can damage the environment around it. **Managing environmental risk** means doing the thinking and the controlling before harm happens.
**Who it is for:** managers and supervisors of hotels, factories, depots, farms, offices, schools and public bodies who are responsible for an organisation's environmental performance.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means at work
rows: List the activities of the business, what each one releases or uses, and the effect on the environment.
Keep a register of laws, permits and conditions; monitor, record and report as required; check before changing the operation.
Rate likelihood and consequence, build a risk register and decide what to treat first.
Use the hierarchy of control and the waste hierarchy; store, handle and dispose of materials safely.
Write and test spill, fire, flood and hurricane plans.
Set targets, use indicators, audit, investigate incidents and review.
Train staff, manage contractors, listen to the community and report to senior managers.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** with workplace scenarios and calculations.
A **written paper**: short answers (exact terms and quick sums) and longer answers in full sentences.
**Group practicals**: an environmental risk assessment and register for a business site, and an emergency procedure with a tabletop exercise. Each member has a named role.

blocks.note: Work every sum twice, and write the formula before you substitute the numbers.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: The part of an activity, product or service that can interact with the environment
Discharging washing water from a paint-mixing tank to a drain
The change in the environment that results, good or bad
Fish dying in a river below the outfall
The chance of harm to the environment (or to the business from the environment) and how bad it would be
A diesel tank leaking into the sea

blocks.note: An **aspect** is something the business does or releases. An **impact** is what happens to the environment because of it. Aspect: waste water. Impact: polluted river.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: An **environmental management system (EMS)** is the structured way an organisation manages its environmental duties, risks and improvement. Most follow the **plan, do, check, act (PDCA)** cycle.

head: Stage
What happens
Examples
rows: Identify aspects, laws and risks; set policy, targets and a programme
Risk register, legal register, target to cut electricity use by 10%
Put the plan into effect: controls, training, equipment, procedures
Spill kits fitted, staff trained, tanks bunded
Measure, monitor, inspect and audit against the plan and the law
Correct problems and improve; management review
Fix causes, update procedures, set new targets

blocks.p: The **environmental policy**, signed by the managing director or most senior manager, should include a commitment to **meet the law, prevent pollution and keep improving**. It gives direction to every plan and target, and it must be communicated to staff and made available to the public where required.

**Senior management is accountable** for making sure environmental risks are managed. Duties are then shared down the line: managers own the risks in their areas, supervisors apply the controls, and every worker follows the rules and reports problems.

head: Type
Examples
rows: Owners, directors, managers, staff, trade unions
Neighbours and residents (for example people living downstream), customers, regulators, insurers, suppliers, contractors, the media, environmental groups

ul: **Prevention is better than cure**: stop pollution at source, which is cheaper than cleaning up.
**Polluter pays**: the organisation that causes pollution bears the cost of putting it right.
**Continual improvement**: each year should be better than the last.
**Precaution**: where harm could be serious and the facts are uncertain, check first and take advice, for example before clearing seagrass or mangroves.

blocks.note: In Jamaica, the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA) is the main environmental regulator. The National Solid Waste Management Authority (NSWMA) collects and disposes of public solid waste. The Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM) co-ordinates disaster preparedness. Always check current requirements with the regulator or an adviser.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: A business must know what it is legally required to do. Laws and permits are described here by their purpose, not by section number; ask the regulator or a qualified adviser for the current details.

blocks.h: What the law and permits usually cover

head: Area
Typical duties
rows: Permission, with conditions, to operate a regulated activity, such as discharging effluent, emitting to air, or developing near the coast or a wetland
Separate hazardous waste, use licensed handlers, keep transfer records
Treat waste water to the standard, test it, keep results
Safe storage, labelling, safety data sheets, spill containment
Approval before major building or changes; an environmental impact assessment (EIA) may be required for large projects near sensitive areas, such as a wetland
Limits on noise, smell and dust affecting neighbours
Rules for beaches, reefs, mangroves, forests and wildlife

blocks.p: Keep a **register of the environmental laws, permits and permit conditions** that apply to the business. For each entry record the requirement, who is responsible, how and when it is checked, and the records kept. This ensures that duties are known, met and checked.

head: Register column
Example
rows: Test the effluent every month and keep the results
Monthly lab report reviewed; filed in the environmental folder

flow: Do the missed activity as soon as possible (for example, test the effluent now)
Record the gap, the reason and the date
Report it to the regulator if the permit or the law requires it
Find the cause (for example, no backup person for the sampler)
Fix the cause so that it does not happen again

blocks.p: If the business expands, adds a process or increases waste, effluent or emissions, **check first whether the permit must be changed or a new one obtained**. Operating beyond the permit is a breach even when the plan is good for business.

ul: Watch official notices and updates from the regulator.
Join industry associations that pass on changes.
Take professional advice when the law is unclear.
Update the register each time something changes, and tell the people affected.

blocks.p: Keep records of monitoring results, waste transfers and collections (signed waste transfer notes show where waste went and that it was handled lawfully), training, inspections, audits, incidents and complaints. Keep them for the period required by the permit, the law or company policy.

flow: List the activities, products and services at the site
For each, identify the aspects (what is used, released or stored)
Identify the possible impacts and who or what could be harmed
Rate the likelihood and the consequence
Calculate the risk score and rank the risks
Decide on controls and the order of action
Record in the risk register and review

blocks.p: Many businesses use a **1 to 5 scale** for each factor.

head: Score
Likelihood
Consequence
rows: Serious; breach of permit, harm to neighbours
Severe; major pollution, serious harm, prosecution

blocks.p: **Risk score = likelihood × consequence**, from 1 to 25. A high score does not always come from a high consequence: rank by the **product**.

head: Risk
Likelihood
Consequence
Score
Priority
rows: Diesel tank leaking into a gully
Paint wash water entering a storm drain

blocks.p: Check each product twice: 3 × 5 = 15, 4 × 3 = 12, 4 × 2 = 8, 5 × 1 = 5.

blocks.note: A risk with a moderate consequence that is almost certain can outrank a severe consequence that is very unlikely. Rank by the score, then use judgement about severe, irreversible harm.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Column
What it holds
rows: What could happen, from which activity
The risk that is left after the controls
What more will be done, by whom and by when

blocks.p: The **residual risk** is the risk that remains after the controls. Review the register at least every year and when anything changes.

ul: **Hurricanes and heavy rain**: flood water carrying stored chemicals into gullies; broken tanks; power failure.
**Low-lying and coastal sites**: sea-level and storm-surge damage; erosion; saltwater.
**Gullies, rivers and the sea** that receive runoff from yards and roads.
**Fuel stores and generators**, which many businesses rely on during power cuts.
**Fragile ecosystems**: coral reefs, seagrass, mangroves, wetlands.
**Drought and water shortage**, which affects supply and the cost of water.
**Old air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment** containing refrigerant gas.
**Waste**: used oil, batteries, fluorescent tubes, e-waste, tyres and food waste.

head: Response
Meaning
Example
rows: Stop the activity that causes the risk
A tour company stops a boat trip that is damaging a coral reef
Add controls to cut likelihood or consequence
Share the risk, for example with insurance or a specialist contractor
Insurance for storm damage; a licensed waste handler
Live with a small risk, and monitor it

blocks.p: Choose controls from the top of the list first.

head: Level
Meaning
Example
rows: Replace it with something less harmful
Change from a solvent cleaner to a water-based cleaner that does the job
Physical changes that contain or reduce the risk
Bunds, oil interceptors, dust extraction, covers, silt fences

blocks.note: Training and PPE protect people but do not stop the release. Put the effort where the risk starts.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Prevent and reduce: make less waste in the first place
Reuse: use again, for example reusable crates from suppliers instead of cardboard
Recycle: turn waste into new materials
Recover: energy or compost from what remains
Dispose: landfill or safe treatment as the last resort

head: Waste
Good practice
rows: Reduce packaging; ask for reusable crates; recycle the rest
Reduce over-ordering; compost or send to farms where lawful
Used oil, batteries, fluorescent tubes, e-waste
Keep apart from general waste; store safely; hand to a licensed handler; keep the transfer note
Have a trained technician recover it for proper handling
Treat as the permit requires; never pour chemicals into storm drains

blocks.h: Storing and handling fuels and chemicals

ul: Keep a **safety data sheet (SDS)** for each chemical: it gives hazards, safe storage and spill advice.
Store tanks and drums in a **bund** (a sealed wall or tray) that can hold a leak and stop it reaching soil or drains.
Label containers; keep incompatible chemicals apart; keep lids closed.
Store on hard standing, under cover, away from drains and flood-prone ground.
Keep a **spill kit** (absorbent pads, booms, bags, gloves) near the store, and keep it stocked.
Fit **oil interceptors** where oily water leaves a vehicle depot.
Train staff **before** they handle chemicals, including spill response.
Buy low-toxicity products where they do the job.
Switch off equipment when not needed; set computers to sleep rather than leave them on overnight.
Use efficient lighting, cooling and appliances; service air-conditioners.
Repair leaks, fit low-flow fittings, harvest rainwater where suitable.
Consider solar water heaters or panels, assessed by their simple payback period.
Where a standby generator runs for long hours, control fumes, noise and fuel leaks.

blocks.h: Noise, dust, smell and other nuisance

ul: Set sound limits; point speakers and equipment away from homes; limit hours.
Wet down or cover dusty areas; use dust extraction; cover trucks.
Check where and when the problem is worst by talking to residents.
Keep a complaints log (see the section on monitoring).

blocks.p: A contractor working for you can create risk for you. Before work starts, check that the **contractor is licensed and disposes of waste lawfully**. Put environmental conditions in the contract, give them your site rules, supervise the work, and keep the waste transfer notes. Buy from suppliers that can show they meet the law.

Before clearing seagrass, mangroves or beach vegetation, or building near the shore, check the **permits first** and get expert advice. Removing these habitats can break the law and increases erosion, flooding and loss of fish nurseries.

blocks.h: Parts of an environmental emergency plan

head: Part
What it covers
rows: Spills, fires, floods, hurricanes, equipment failure
Who leads, who contains the spill, who calls, who records
Stop the source, raise the alarm, protect people
Block drains, use the spill kit, build a bund of sand or absorbent
Where kits, absorbents, pumps and PPE are kept
Emergency services (110 for fire and ambulance), the regulator, the licensed cleaner, the managing director, neighbours
What must be reported, to whom and by when

flow: Protect people and raise the alarm; keep everyone clear
Stop the leak at the source if it is safe to do so
Contain it: block the drain and surround the spill with the spill kit
Call for help, and inform the manager
Clean up using absorbents; store contaminated material safely
Report to the authority and neighbours as required
Investigate the root cause and update the controls

blocks.note: Example: a drum of used oil splits during heavy rain and oil runs toward a storm drain. The first action is to **block the drain and contain the oil**, not to wash it away with water.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Test the plan with **drills and tabletop exercises**. They show whether staff know their roles and expose gaps in the plan, such as missing equipment or wrong phone numbers.
The Atlantic hurricane season runs from 1 June to 30 November.

head: When
Actions
rows: Check drains, roofs and tanks; review the plan; train staff; stock spill kits and supplies

Secure or remove loose items; move chemicals and fuel to safe high ground, sealed and labelled; shut down and isolate equipment; top up and secure generators; back up records; tell staff, neighbours and contractors the plan
Stay safe; do not take risks to protect property
Check for leaks, damage, flood contamination and unsafe electrics before restarting; clean up and dispose of debris and waste lawfully; report as required; review lessons

blocks.p: A **near miss** is an event that could have caused harm but did not, such as a chemical drum that nearly toppled. Encourage staff to report near misses so causes are fixed before real harm is done.
After an incident:

ol: Make safe, contain and clean up.
Record the facts: what, where, when, how much, who was involved.
Report as required by law or permit.
Find the **root cause** by asking why repeatedly, not just the first cause (for example, why was the drum placed there?).
Agree actions, owners and dates, and update the controls and training.
Share the lessons and check that the actions worked.

blocks.note: If a worker tells you that she poured bleach down the storm drain, record and report the incident and arrange retraining. Blame alone will stop others from reporting.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: A good target is **specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound**: for example *cut electricity per room night by 10% by December*. Use indicators that allow for busy and quiet periods, such as **per occupied room night** or **per unit produced**.

head: Indicator
Formula
Worked example
rows: waste recycled or composted ÷ total waste × 100

ul: **Monitoring**: routine measuring, such as effluent tests, meter readings, waste records and inspections.
**Internal audit**: a planned check of whether controls and duties are being met, carried out by trained people who are independent of the area audited.
Check **more often** where the risk score is higher.
Record findings, set corrective actions with owners and dates, and verify they are done.

head: Audit finding
Corrective action
rows: Restock now; add a monthly check to the inspection sheet
Train the staff; keep records and a refresher timetable
Obtain copies; give one person responsibility for filing

blocks.p: Senior managers should review the system at least every year: audit findings, incidents, complaints, results against targets, changes in law and risk, and resources. They then set new targets and approve funding. A strong case to the board is that a control **cuts the risk of pollution, fines and clean-up costs**.

flow: Record the complaint: who, when, what, where
Acknowledge it promptly
Investigate the cause
Take action to stop or reduce the problem
Reply to the person with what you found and did
Review complaint patterns to improve controls

blocks.p: When neighbours complain about a smell, noise or dust, record the details, investigate and reply. For a regular problem, such as dust from a site, **meet residents** to find out when and where it is worst. Keep a complaints log and review it.

ul: Train new staff before they start the work; refresh regularly.
Brief night-shift and part-time staff in person, give a copy of the procedure and check they understand.
Explain **why** the rule exists, not only what it is.
Involve staff in finding solutions and recognise good practice.
Supervisors check, correct and set the example.

blocks.note: Staff ignore rules they do not understand or that make work harder. Ask them what makes waste separation difficult (bins in the wrong place, too few bins), fix that, then enforce.
blocks.label: Tip

The change in the environment that results
Written permission, with conditions, to carry out a regulated activity
Waste water discharged from a factory or plant

Order of preference: eliminate, substitute, engineer, administer, PPE

c1.title: A furniture factory in Kingston
c1.text: A furniture factory in Kingston's industrial area has rated four risks on 1 to 5 scales. Spray-finishing vapour: likelihood 4, consequence 2. Finishing wash water entering a gully: likelihood 3, consequence 4. A solvent store fire: likelihood 2, consequence 5. Wood offcuts left in the yard: likelihood 5, consequence 1. Sanding also produces fine wood dust that workers breathe.

c2.title: A Negril hotel's energy, water and waste figures
c2.text: A 300-room hotel in Negril used 3,600,000 litres (3,600 m³) of water in a month, with 6,000 occupied room nights. After repairing leaks, monthly water use fell from 3,600 m³ to 3,060 m³. The hotel produced 25 tonnes of waste in a month and recycled or composted 10 tonnes. Solar water heaters cost J$4,500,000 and will save J$900,000 a year.

c3.title: A Treasure Beach guest house before and after a hurricane
c3.text: A guest house in Treasure Beach stores pool chemicals and a drum of diesel for its generator near the sea wall. A hurricane warning has been issued for the south coast. The guest house has a septic tank, and the owner, Marcia Gordon, wants to reopen as soon as the storm passes.

c4.title: A building site in the Corporate Area
c4.text: A contractor is building offices in the Corporate Area. Neighbours complain of dust each morning from 7:00 a.m. and of muddy runoff reaching a storm drain after rain. The site uses a subcontractor to remove excavated soil. The site manager has logged six complaints in a month.

c5.title: An internal audit at a food processor in Clarendon
c5.text: A food processor in Clarendon has an environmental management system. An internal audit finds that the spill kit is empty, the effluent test results are complete and filed, two night-shift staff have no spill training records, and the environmental policy is displayed only in the head office.

questions.q: What is the risk score of the finishing wash water entering the gully?
questions.why: Risk score = likelihood × consequence = 3 × 4 = 12. Adding the scores (7) is not the method.

questions.q: Which risk should the factory manager treat first?
o: Wood offcuts left in the yard (score 5)
Spray-finishing vapour in the shop (score 8)
Wash water into the gully (score 12)
The solvent store fire in the yard (score 10)
questions.why: The scores are 12, 10, 8 and 5, so the wash water ranks first, even though the fire has the highest consequence. Rank by the product, then use judgement about severe harm.

questions.q: For the wood dust from sanding, which control is highest in the hierarchy of control?
o: Issue dust masks to every worker who sands
Fit dust extraction at the sanding bench
Put up a sign asking workers to keep clear
Train the sanders to sand more slowly each day
questions.why: Engineering controls, such as extraction at the source, rank above administrative controls and PPE. A mask protects only the wearer and leaves dust in the workshop and the air.

questions.q: The manager adds a bund and a fire-rated cabinet to the solvent store. What is the risk that remains afterwards called?
o: Inherent risk
Residual risk
Environmental aspect
Likelihood
questions.why: Residual risk is the risk left after the controls are in place. It should be rated again and reviewed.

questions.q: How many litres of water were used per occupied room night?
questions.why: Litres per room night = 3,600,000 ÷ 6,000 = 600. Check: 600 × 6,000 = 3,600,000. The indicator allows for busy and quiet months.

questions.q: What was the percentage reduction in monthly water use after the repairs?
What share of the hotel's waste was kept out of landfill?
questions.why: 10 ÷ 25 × 100 = 40%. Check: 40% of 25 = 10. The base is total waste.

questions.q: A supplier says the solar water heaters last about 8 years. What does this suggest, given the figures?
o: They never pay back, because 8 years is too long to wait
They pay back in 8 years, which is exactly their life
They pay back in 5 years, then save for 3 more
Payback cannot be judged without knowing the hotel's profit
questions.why: Payback = 4,500,000 ÷ 900,000 = 5 years, which is inside the 8-year life, so the heaters save about 3 years of cost (3 × J$900,000 = J$2,700,000) after paying for themselves.

questions.q: What should the owner do with the pool chemicals and the diesel drum before the hurricane?
o: Leave them near the sea wall in their own containers
Move them to high, secure ground, sealed and labelled
Pour the diesel into the septic tank to get rid of it
Pile them by the front gate for removal after the storm
questions.why: Flood and storm surge can carry chemicals and fuel into the sea or the gully. Moving them above flood level, sealed and labelled, reduces the risk.

questions.q: After the storm, Marcia wants to reopen at once. What should she do first?
o: Check for leaks, damage and contamination first
Reopen and check the septic tank when guests complain
Wash any spilt chemicals away into the sea
Skip the checks so that guests are not kept waiting
questions.why: After a storm there may be leaking tanks, damaged septic systems, flood contamination and unsafe electrics. Check and make safe before restarting.

questions.q: Why should the guest house have rehearsed its plan during a drill before the season?
o: To meet a rule about the colour of safety signs
To reduce the number of staff that are needed
To avoid having to write a plan for each risk
To check people know their roles and to find gaps
questions.why: Drills and exercises show whether the plan works in practice and reveal gaps such as missing equipment or contacts.

questions.q: Which action best controls the muddy runoff reaching the storm drain?
o: Wash the mud into the drain with a hose each day
Ask the neighbours to clear the storm drain
Stop logging complaints so that fewer are recorded
Install silt fences and cover the soil stockpiles
questions.why: Engineering controls at source, such as silt fences and covered soil, stop sediment leaving the site. Washing mud into the drain only moves the problem.

questions.q: What should the site manager check before the subcontractor starts removing soil?
o: That it offers the lowest price of all the bidders
That its trucks are the newest ones in the parish
That it is licensed and disposes of the soil lawfully
That it is willing to carry out the work at night
questions.why: A contractor's illegal dumping is a risk to your business. Check the licence and disposal, put the conditions in the contract and keep the records.

questions.q: Six complaints in a month, most about dust at 7:00 a.m. What is the best use of the complaints log?
o: Reply to each caller once and then file the notes
Find the pattern and the cause, and act on it
Move the log to the head office for safe keeping
Count them and report only the total each month
questions.why: A complaints log shows when and where problems occur. The pattern, here early morning dust, points to a cause such as dry soil or early trucks, and to a control such as wetting down.

questions.q: What is the best first step to reduce the early-morning dust?
o: Meet residents and see when and where dust is worst
Close the site and move the project elsewhere
Tell residents to keep their windows closed
Wait for the next complaint before taking any step
questions.why: Listening to the community and observing the site finds the cause. Then controls, such as wetting the surface and changing truck times, can be tested.

questions.q: Which audit finding should the manager correct first?
o: The empty spill kit
The policy displayed only in the head office
The completed effluent test records
The colour of the filing cabinets
questions.why: A spill kit that is empty means that a leak cannot be contained, which is a direct risk. The policy display and training records also need action, but the kit is the most urgent.

questions.q: Two night-shift staff have no spill training. What should the manager do?
o: Wait for the yearly review to add them to training
Ask day staff to handle the chemicals at night
Accept that night-shift staff are exempt from training
Train them and keep records before they handle chemicals
questions.why: Staff must be trained before they handle chemicals. Night-shift staff are covered by the same rules.

questions.q: The audit is part of which stage of the plan-do-check-act cycle?
o: Plan
Do
Check
Act
questions.why: Auditing measures results against the plan and the law, which is the check stage. The corrective actions that follow belong to the act stage.

questions.q: A large hotel plans a new development beside a wetland. The authority may first ask for a study of its likely effects. What is this called?
o: A waste hierarchy review for the site
An environmental impact assessment (EIA)
A risk register for the new building
An internal audit of the existing hotel
questions.why: An EIA assesses the likely effects of a project and how to avoid or reduce them before it is approved.

questions.q: A business buys insurance against storm damage to its fuel store. Which response to risk is this?
o: Terminating the risk
Transferring the risk
Accepting the risk
Eliminating the aspect
questions.why: Insurance moves some of the financial consequences to the insurer. It does not remove the risk, so controls are still needed.
